extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and educated readers/critics (Elizabethan-era writers and dramatists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for composing poetry and drama (verse, diction, comic/tragic form, meter and rhetorical devices), with examples and common abuses noted drawing on classical precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy bound to poesy not history
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is tied to the laws of poesy, and not of history; not bound to follow the story, but having liberty either to feign a quite new matter, or to frame the history to the most tragical convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may compress or adapt historical facts for tragic effect; they need not slavishly reproduce historical chronology or geography. Use the liberty to shape events to the tragic necessities of passion and unity rather than to literal historic sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin at the principal point (not ab ovo)
rubrics_metrics.description: When representing a history, they must not, as Horace saith, begin 'ab ovo', but they must come to the principal point of that one action which they will represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the play at the crucial, most tragic moment (example: Euripides begins Polydorus with the finding of the body rather than with the child's delivery). Avoid dramatizing irrelevant earlier episodes that waste time and diffuse focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narration/messengers for off-stage or remote events
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things may be told, which cannot be showed: the ancients took by some 'Nuntius' to recount things done in former time, or other place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where events cannot reasonably be staged (far places, long periods), employ narrators/messengers to report them rather than attempt implausible stage representation. This preserves plausibility and economy of drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain coherence of place and time for audience conceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays that shift many places and many times without credible representation force the audience to be told where they are or else the tale will not be conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid random, jarring scene switches and inconsistent props (e.g., garden → rock → cave → battlefield simulated with inadequate devices). Ensure stage representation is coherent enough that spectators can accept the fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve genre decency; avoid improper mingling of kings and clowns
rubrics_metrics.description: All their plays be neither right tragedies nor right comedies, mingling kings and clowns, not because the matter so carrieth it, but thrust in the clown by head and shoulders to play a part in majestical matters, with neither decency nor discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert crude comic buffoonery into high tragic scenes merely to provoke laughter. Maintain appropriate tone and decorum for each genre; the tragic should sustain admiration, the comic should sustain delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should teach delight; avoid scurrility and mocking the pitiable
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the comical part be not upon such scornful matters as stir laughter only, but mix with it that delightful teaching which is the end of poesy. They stir laughter in sinful things, which are rather execrable than ridiculous; or in miserable, which are rather to be pitied than scorned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid laughter at the expense of the poor, the miserable, or through contemptuous cruelty (e.g., jesting at beggars or mocking strangers' speech). Aim for comic characters and situations that instruct and delight (e.g., busy courtier, self-wise schoolmaster), not mere scurrility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish delight from laughter; aim for instructive delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Delight and laughter are not identical: delight relates to what is convenient to ourselves or nature, laughter to what is disproportionate; both may co-occur but are different in kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing comic elements, ensure they also produce the 'delightful teaching' proper to poesy rather than only provoking scornful laughter. Use contrast and mixed effects (examples: Alexander's portrait, Hercules at Omphale) judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid far-fetched diction and painted affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The outside of poetry, which is words or diction, is often worse: honey-flowing matron eloquence, apparelled or disguised in a courtesan-like painted affectation; far-fetched words that make many seem monsters or strangers to English readers; figures and flowers extremely winter-starved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, intelligible diction over extravagant vocabulary or ostentatious rhetorical ornament. Do not burden verse with obscure or excessively learned words that alienate ordinary listeners/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical figures sparingly and for persuasion (hide art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators who merely keep notebooks of figures and phrases bring art to show art, not hide art. Rhetorical devices should serve persuasion—the chief mark of oratory—not curiosity of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing examples (e.g., repetition used by Cicero) is permissible but should be controlled. Employ repetition, cadence, and other devices when they arise organically from passion or purpose; do not parade them for display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit similitudes and stock examples; avoid surfeit
rubrics_metrics.description: Many printed discourses rifle up herbalists, stories of beasts, fowls, and fishes so that similitudes come in multitudes—a surfeit to the ears. The force of a similitude is to explain to a willing hearer; beyond that it is tedious prattling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors and similes only as necessary to clarify or illuminate; excessive or irrelevant similitudes distract and overwhelm the listener's memory and the argument's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose meter and rhyme to suit purpose; English fits both ancient and modern modes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two sorts of versifying: the ancient (quantity-based) and the modern (number/accent/rhyme-based). The ancient is more fit for music and expressive variety of passions; the modern, with rhyme, strikes a certain music to the ear. English is fit for both and has advantages (precise accent, caesura, variety of masculine/feminine/sdrucciola rhymes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metrical form by desired effect: quantity for musicality and passion, rhyme for sweet sounding and popular delight. Observe accent and caesura carefully; exploit English's rhythmic possibilities rather than forcing foreign metrical habits ill-suited to the tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clear expression of conceit over rigid grammar or affected mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: Though some say English is a mingled language or lacks grammar, it is capable of 'uttering sweetly and properly the conceit of the mind.' Grammar might be present but is not an excuse for obscurity; the end of speech is to utter the conceit plainly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on clarity and natural expression so that the reader/hearer perceives the poet's thought. Avoid defensive appeals to language 'defects'—instead shape words to make conceits immediately intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use genuine feeling in love-poetry; avoid stock 'swelling phrases'
rubrics_metrics.description: Many love-writings apply fiery speeches coldly, as men who caught certain swelling phrases from reading; they hang together like a man who lists winds because he will name winds enough rather than reveal true passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In lyric and sonnet writing, rely on true passion and force ('energia') rather than cliché phrases. The material (praise of immortal beauty, goodness, God) is abundant—use it with sincere feeling rather than mechanical imitation.
